Android from the foundation · Puzzle 4 of 6

system_server is the town hall

One long-running process holds Android's system services. It keeps the register of every app and screen, and it decides their lifecycle, not your app.

The problem

If every app is locked in its own sandbox, who decides which app is on screen, who may use the camera, which app handles a link, and which app to kill when memory runs low? It has to be one trusted place that sees everything.

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

system_server is a process started at boot that runs as long as the phone is on. Inside it live the system services: the activity and task managers (screens, tasks, process priority), the package manager (installed apps, their components, permissions), the window manager (what's on screen and who gets touches), and many more.

It starts in SystemServer.main()system_server's entry point: it starts the bootstrap services (activities, packages, power…). 684 public static void main(String[] args) { 685 new SystemServer().run(); … 976 startBootstrapServices(t);SystemServer.java, line 684 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗. When your app calls startActivity(), the request arrives in ActivityTaskManagerService.startActivity()Where your startActivity() lands inside system_server, after crossing Binder. 1226 public final int startActivity(IApplicationThread caller, String callingPackage, … 1230 return startActivityAsUser(caller, callingPackage, callingFeatureId, intent, resolvedType,ActivityTaskManagerService.java, line 1226 · AOSP frameworks/base ↗.

It keeps a record of every screen of every app, and tells your app when to create, pause, stop or destroy one.

The analogy

The town hall keeps the official register of every flat and resident. You don't issue your own building permit; you ask, and they send you the decision.
